source_text: Quod si dei ac per hoc rationis quoque compotes agerent, merita primo paenitentiae expenderent, nec unquam eam ad argumentum perversae emendationis adhiberent; modum denique paenitendi temperarent, quia et delinquendi tenerent, timentes dominum scilicet. Sed ubi metus nullus, emendatio proinde nulla: ubi emendatio nulla, paenitentia necessario vana; quia caret fructu suo cui eam deus sevit, id est hominis saluti. Nam deus post tot ac tanta delicta humanae temeritatis a principe generis Adam auspicata, post condemnatum hominem cum saeculi dote, post eiectum paradiso mortique subiectum, cum rursus ad suam misericordiam maturavisset, iam inde in semetipso paenitentiam dedicavit, rescissa sententia irarum pristinarum, ignoscere pactus operi et imagini suae. Itaque et populum sibi congregavit, et multis bonitatis suae largitionibus fovit, et ingratissimum totiens expertus ad paenitentiam semper hortatus est, et prophetando universorum prophetarum emisit ora: mox gratiam pollicitus, quam in extremitatibus temporum per spiritum suum universo orbi illuminaturus esset, praeire intinctionem paenitentiae iussit, si quos per gratiam vocaret ad promissionem semini Abraham destinatam per paenitentiae subsignationem ante componeret. Non tacet Ioannes, Paenitentiam initote, dicens, iam enim salus nationibus appropinquabit, dominus scilicet, afferens secundum dei promissum. Cui praeministrans paenitentiam destinabat purgandis mentibus praepositam, uti quicquid error vetus inquinasset, quicquid in corde hominis ignorantia contaminasset, id paenitentia verrens et radens et foras abiciens mundam pectoris domum superventuro spiritui sancto paret, quo se ille cum caelestibus bonis libens inferat. Horum bonorum unus est titulus, salus hominis, criminum pristinorum abolitione praemissa. Haec paenitentiae causa, haec opera negotium divinae misericordiae curans. Quod homini proficit, deo servit. Ceterum ratio eius, quam cognito domino discimus, certam formam tenet, ne bonis unquam factis cogitatisve quasi violenta aliqua manus iniciatur. Deus enim reprobationem bonorum ratam non habens, utpote suorum, quorum cum auctor, et defensor sit necesse est, proinde et acceptator, si acceptator, etiam remunerator. Viderit ergo ingratia hominum, si etiam bonis factis paenitentiam cogit. Viderit et gratia, si captatio eius ad benefaciendum incitamento est, terrena, mortalis utraque. Quantulum enim compendii, si grato benefeceris? vel dispendii, si ingrato? Bonum factum deum habet debitorem, sicuti et malum, quia iudex omnis remunerator est causae. At cum index deus iustitiae carissimae sibi exigendae tuendaeque praesideat, et in eam omnem summam disciplinae suae sanciat, dubitandum est, sicut in universis actibus nostris, ita in paenitentiae quoque causa iustitiam deo praestandam esse? quod quidem ita impleri licebit, si peccatis solummodo adhibeatur. Porro peccatum nisi malum factum dici non meretur, nec quisquam benefaciendo delinquit. Quodsi non delinquit, cur paenitentiam invadit, delinquentium privatum? Cur malitiae officium bonitati suae imponit? Ita evenit, ut, cum aliquid ubi non oportet adhibetur, illic ubi oportet neglegatur.
thought_title: Repentance belongs only to sins, not to good deeds
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that repentance must be directed only toward sins, never toward good deeds, and he now grounds this in God's own purpose for repentance.
pass_a_gloss: But if they acted as those in possession of God and therefore also of reason, they would first weigh the merits of repentance, and they would never apply it as a proof of perverse correction; finally they would set a limit to repenting, because they would also hold a limit to sinning, fearing the Lord, of course. But where there is no fear of God, correction is likewise none: where correction is none, repentance is necessarily empty; because it lacks its fruit for which God sowed it, that is, for the salvation of man. For God, after so many and so great sins of human rashness begun from the first parent Adam, after man was condemned with the endowment of the world, after he was cast out of paradise and subjected to death, when he had again hastened to his mercy, from then on dedicated repentance in himself, the sentence of former wrath having been rescinded, having covenanted to forgive his work and his image. And so he also gathered a people to himself, and cherished them with many bounties of his goodness, and having experienced them most ungrateful so often, he always urged them to repentance, and by prophesying he sent forth the mouths of all the prophets: soon he promised grace, which in the last times through his spirit he would shed light upon the whole world, he commanded the baptism of repentance to go before, so that if he should call any through grace to the promise destined to the seed of Abraham, he would first prepare them through the sealing of repentance. John does not keep silent, saying: Begin repentance, for now salvation will draw near to the nations, the Lord, of course, bringing it according to the promise of God. Ministering to him, he appointed repentance set over minds to be cleansed, so that whatever old error had defiled, whatever ignorance had contaminated in the heart of man, repentance sweeping and scraping and casting it out of doors might prepare a clean house of the breast for the Holy Spirit about to come, into which he might gladly bring himself with heavenly goods. Of these goods one is the title, the salvation of man, with the abolition of former crimes having been sent ahead. This is the cause of repentance, this is its work, attending to the business of divine mercy. What profits man, serves God. Moreover its method, which we learn when the Lord is known, holds a fixed form, that a hand, as it were violent, should never be laid upon good deeds done or thought. For God, not holding the rejection of good things as valid, inasmuch as they are his own, of which since he is the author, he must also be the defender, and likewise the acceptor, if the acceptor, also the rewarder. Let the ingratitude of men see to it, if it forces repentance even upon good deeds. Let gratitude also see to it, if its pursuit is an incitement to doing good, both earthly, both mortal. For how little is the gain, if you do good to a grateful person? or the loss, if to an ungrateful one? A good deed has God as debtor, just as also an evil one, because the judge is the rewarder of every case. But since God the judge presides over justice most dear to him, to be exacted and defended, and sanctions it as the whole sum of his discipline, is it to be doubted that, just as in all our acts, so also in the matter of repentance justice must be rendered to God? which indeed will be allowed to be fulfilled in this way, if it is applied to sins only. Furthermore sin does not deserve to be called anything but an evil deed, nor does anyone sin by doing good. But if he does not sin, why does he lay hold of repentance, which is the private property of sinners? Why does he impose the office of wickedness upon his goodness? So it happens that, when something is applied where it is not fitting, it is neglected there where it is fitting.

choices.why: Keeps the sense of God establishing repentance as a fixed institution in himself, matching the legal-covenantal tone of the passage.

choices.why: Uses the glossary rendering for intinctio and keeps the genitive relationship, matching the biblical phrase Tertullian echoes.
Renders the rare noun literally as the act of sealing, preserving the image of baptism as a mark or seal preparatory to the promise.
Renders privatum as a substantive adjective meaning what belongs exclusively to sinners, keeping the legal-ownership metaphor.
Keeps officium as a duty or function, preserving the paradox of imposing wickedness's task on goodness.

bible_refs.note: Paenitentiam initote, iam enim salus nationibus appropinquabit

pass_b_english: But if people had God, and therefore reason as well, they would first weigh what repentance deserves. They would never use it as a device for perverse correction. They would at least set a limit to their repenting, because they would also hold a limit to their sinning, since they fear the Lord. But where there is no fear of God, there is likewise no amendment. Where there is no amendment, repentance is necessarily empty, because it lacks the fruit for which God sowed it, namely human salvation.

For after so many and such great sins of human recklessness, begun with Adam the first of our race, after man was condemned along with the world's endowment, after he was cast out of paradise and made subject to death, God then hastened back to his own mercy. From that point on he dedicated repentance in himself. The sentence of his former wrath was rescinded, and he covenanted to forgive his own work and image. And so he gathered a people to himself and nourished them with many gifts of his goodness. Though he found them utterly ungrateful time and again, he always urged them to repentance. Through the mouths of all the prophets he spoke, soon promising the grace with which he would illuminate the whole world through his Spirit at the end of the ages. He commanded the baptism of repentance to go before, so that if he called any through grace to the promise destined for Abraham's seed, he might first prepare them through the sealing of repentance.

John the Baptist does not keep silent. He says, "Begin repentance, for salvation is now drawing near to the nations," meaning the Lord who brings it according to God's promise. Ministering to him, John appointed repentance to be set over minds that needed cleansing, so that whatever old error had defiled, whatever ignorance had contaminated in the human heart, repentance might sweep it, scrape it, and cast it out. It would prepare a clean house of the breast for the Holy Spirit who was about to come upon it, so that he might gladly bring himself in with heavenly goods. One title of these goods is human salvation, with the abolition of former sins sent ahead. This is the cause of repentance, this its work, attending to the business of divine mercy. Whatever benefits a human being is what serves God.

Moreover, the rule of repentance, which we learn once we have come to know the Lord, holds to a fixed form: it must never lay violent hands, so to speak, on good deeds or good thoughts. For God does not hold the rejection of good things as valid, since they are his own. As their author and defender, he must also be their acceptor, and if their acceptor, then also their rewarder. Let human ingratitude see to it, then, if it plans repentance even for good deeds. Let gratitude see to it too, if courting it is an incentive to doing good. Both are earthly and mortal. How small is the gain if you do good to a grateful person, or the loss if to an ungrateful one? A good deed has God as its debtor, just as an evil deed does, because every judge is the rewarder of a case.

But since God the judge presides over justice, which he holds dearest and demands and defends, and since he ordains the whole sum of his discipline toward it, can there be any doubt that in the matter of repentance, as in all our actions, justice must be rendered to God? And this can only be fulfilled if repentance is applied to sins alone. For sin does not deserve to be called anything but an evil deed, and no one sins by doing good. But if he does not sin, why does he seize upon repentance, the private property of sinners? Why does he impose the office of wickedness on his own goodness? So it happens that when something is applied where it should not be, it is neglected where it should be.

last_rejected.why: 'dos' here means dowry/portion, not 'endowment'; Adam was condemned with the world's dowry.
last_rejected.ruling: "saeculi dote" = gift/endowment of the world; "world's endowment" fits Latin sense, not a meaning‑changing error

problems.quote: What benefits a human being serves God.
problems.why: Reads like a fragment or mistranslation; the meaning seems to be 'Whatever benefits a human being is what serves God' or 'What serves God benefits a human being.'
problems.fix: Reconstruct as 'Whatever benefits a human being is what serves God.'

problems.quote: Begin repentance, for salvation is now drawing near to the nations
problems.why: Matthew 3:2 says 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand'; 'salvation drawing near to the nations' does not match the cited verse.
problems.fix: Note that Tertullian paraphrases or cites an Old Latin variant; the sense is close but not verbatim Matthew 3:2.

edits.old: What benefits a human being serves God.
edits.new: Whatever benefits a human being is what serves God.

fixed: Changed 'What benefits a human being serves God' to 'Whatever benefits a human being is what serves God' because the source 'Quod homini proficit, deo servit' means 'That which profits man serves God' — the relative clause 'quod homini proficit' is the subject, not an interrogative. The original English read as a fragment or question.

The scripture citation Matthew 3:2 was not changed: Tertullian's Old Latin text reads 'Paenitentiam initote, iam enim salus nationibus appropinquabit', which is a paraphrase or variant of Matthew 3:2 ('Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand'). The English accurately renders Tertullian's wording, and the citation is appropriate as a reference to the passage Tertullian is drawing on.

polish.changed: Clarified the meaning of the fragment about benefiting a human being and serving God, removed the incorrect Matthew 3:2 citation, and smoothed sentence order and pronoun references throughout for natural modern reading.
